title: Hither Woods: Refuge, Land Agreements and Continuing Rights
summary: A Montaukett agreement made during displacement helped English East Hampton claim Hither Woods, but also preserved Native houses, firewood and protections for planted corn. Its promises and restrictions show how land control changed without ending Native relationships.

why_this_matters: The same document that supported English possession also preserved Montaukett homes, resources and an obligation to provide refuge. Those terms make continuing Native rights and colonial restrictions visible together.
introduction_title: Refuge, obligations and a continuing homeland
introduction_content: A Montaukett agreement made during displacement helped English East Hampton claim Hither Woods, but also preserved Native houses, firewood and protections for planted corn. Its promises and restrictions show how land control changed without ending Native relationships.
history_title: The agreement and the rights within it
history_content:
A homeland between Napeague and Montauk

Hither Woods is the wooded western part of the Montauk peninsula, east of Napeague and extending toward Fort Pond. It is part of Montaukett homeland. Its land history includes a distinct agreement in 1661/62, before the later transactions farther east and long before the 1879 Montauk auction. Reading these as separate events shows how English control expanded through successive agreements and restrictions, while Montaukett people continued to live on and use their homeland. Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island

Refuge and an unequal setting for an agreement

The agreement followed violence and displacement. Its own account says that Montaukett people had fled conflict involving Ninnicraft and found refuge among the English inhabitants of East Hampton. The Native parties named at its beginning are the Sunk Squa, the widow of Wiandanch, her son Wionkombone, and chief counsellor Pokkatonn, with their associates. The document also names Lion Gardiner and David Gardiner as guardians appointed for Wionkombone by his father. A History of the Town of East-Hampton, N.Y.

East Hampton was an English colonial settlement. The agreement refers back to an earlier instrument involving English settlers Thomas Baker, Robert Bond, Thomas James, Lion Gardiner, John Mulford, John Hand and Benjamin Price and their associates. It presents the new grant to participating East Hampton inhabitants as gratitude for shelter. That is how the document describes the transaction; it cannot, by itself, establish what every Montaukett participant understood or erase the pressure created by having to seek safety away from home. A History of the Town of East-Hampton, N.Y.

The deed did not simply end Native life on the land

The written grant promised enduring possession to East Hampton inhabitants and their successors. Yet the same document preserved Montaukett rights to build houses west of the pond and obtain firewood there. It required the English to maintain a fence on the north side of the pond and Native people to secure the south side against cattle while their corn was growing. English cattle could range eastward after the growing season under the earlier arrangement. These provisions describe continuing residence, planting and negotiated use, not an empty landscape changing hands. A History of the Town of East-Hampton, N.Y.

There were also restrictions. The agreement prevented Montaukett parties from giving, leasing or selling the eastern land without East Hampton's consent. It connected shelter and access to English control over future transactions. If war, sickness or other danger made staying on Montauk unsafe, surviving community members were to be allowed to return to East Hampton for shelter and be provided with land under the former agreement. That obligation belongs in the story alongside the grant. A History of the Town of East-Hampton, N.Y.

Why the language of ownership matters

An English deed could turn a relationship involving refuge, obligations and shared use into a claim of permanent property for the recipients and their heirs. Here the written terms themselves preserve Native homes, fuel gathering and planted corn while establishing English control. The difference matters: a document labeled a grant is not sufficient evidence that Native people surrendered every relationship or right. Nor should we assume one uniform Native understanding of all deeds; the particular terms and circumstances have to be read. A History of the Town of East-Hampton, N.Y.

A continuing homeland, not a completed disappearance

The later history includes pressure on families at Indian Fields and Montaukett survival. The Hither Woods story is one stage in that history, not the end of a people. Continue to the Montauk auction and Indian Fields articles for those later events and their sources. Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island

LandBack asks what restoring Indigenous authority and relationships with land can mean today. In California, the Indigenous women-led Sogorea Te’ Land Trust describes rematriation through renewed relationships with ancestral land, language and ceremony. It provides one model, not a single policy for every Native nation. What is Rematriation? For this place, the historical record gives concrete questions to ask: whose use was protected, whose future choices were restricted, and which obligations were promised? This map does not announce a Hither Woods land return or speak for Montaukett communities about a current proposal. Contemporary restoration should be led by the communities concerned.

The record is dated February 11, 1661 under the old-style year convention. This chapter uses 1661/62; the historical map labels the agreement 1662. The timeline uses the year rather than asserting a converted calendar day.

whereintheworld_content: The outline follows the modern coastal landscape from the highlands east of Napeague Harbor toward Fort Pond. It is a reading area, not a recovered 1661/62 survey, a park boundary or a public-access invitation. The connecting western edge and the eastern edge near Fort Pond are approximate. The outline excludes North Neck, associated with later transactions. Fort Pond is distinct from the separate modern Fresh Pond in Hither Woods.
